item.title: Dropdown Navigation Needs Structure and Feedback
item.description: A dropdown menu is not just a place to hide links. It needs clear grouping, readable spacing, and current-state feedback so users know where they are and where they can go next.

item.title: Customer-Facing Pages Should Not Show the Strategy
item.description: A website can be built for SEO, AI search, conversion, and authority without telling visitors about the strategy. Buyers need answers, not behind-the-scenes labels.

item.title: Operational History Beats Generic About Pages
item.description: Most About pages are too vague. A stronger company history section turns real milestones, operational depth, and capacity into trust.

item.title: Process Photos Beat People Photos When Buyers Need Proof
item.description: Buyer-focused websites should use photos that prove capability. For technical businesses, process photos often build more trust than generic people photos.

item.title: Hero Sections Should Earn the Scroll
item.description: A homepage hero should do more than look good. It should make the offer obvious, show proof, guide the next click, and transition cleanly into the page.

item.title: Location Sections Should Sell Capacity
item.description: A location section should do more than list addresses. Use it to explain reach, capacity, trust, and the next step a buyer should take.

item.title: Proof Blocks Beat Generic Stats
item.description: Website stats work better when they explain why a buyer should care. Turn simple numbers into proof blocks that connect experience, capacity, process, and fit.

item.title: Why Most Professional Websites Fail to Establish Authority in 3 Seconds
item.description: Most professional websites bury their best credibility signal below the fold. Here's why above-the-fold authority positioning is the highest-leverage change you can make — and how to do it.
